title: Plugin sandbox permission tokens — sketch
content:
Purpose
-----
Quick personal sketch for a lightweight permission/token model for sandboxed plugins (extensions that run untrusted or semi-trusted code inside the runtime). Goal: small, audit-friendly tokens that express a narrow capability surface, can be minted by control-plane, and validated cheaply in the edge/host runtime.

Requirements / constraints
- Minimal runtime overhead: token verification should be <= 1 crypto op for the common case.
- Expressivity: allow granting filesystem-read, network-egress to specific hosts, quota for CPU slices, safe tool-call allowances.
- Revocation: support short TTLs + revocation lists for emergency revoke.
- Auditable: token contains stable identifier and human-readable intent string for logs.
- Offline validation: host might be disconnected; graceful degradation is acceptable if token TTL expired.

High-level shape (text-first API)
- Token envelope (compact JWT-like but not standard JWT):
  - header: v=1, alg=ed25519, kid=ctl-01
  - payload fields (compact keys):
    - sub: plugin:<tenant>:<plugin-id>
    - iat: unix_ts
    - exp: unix_ts
    - scope: csv of capability atoms (fs:r:/path, net:e:https://api.example.com, run:toolX)
    - q: numeric quota token (optional, integer)
    - audit: short human reason string (max 128 chars)
    - nonce: short random string for replay protection optional
  - sig: ed25519(signature over header.payload)

Notes on capability atoms
- fs:r:/path (read-only subtree) or fs:w:/tmp/sandbox (write allowed only to specific containment dirs). Use path prefix semantics.
- net:e:host[:port][:scheme] (eg net:e:api.stripe.com:443:https) — a shorthand permit for egress; wildcard host allowed only by explicit control-plane opt-in.
- run:tool-name[:args-hash] — allows invocation of registered host tools with optional arg-hash to constrain inputs.

Compact textual example
---
HEADER:v1;ALG:ed25519;KID:ctl-01|PAYLOAD:sub=plugin:acme:spellcheck;iat=1700000000;exp=1700003600;scope=fs:r:/data/plugins/acme,net:e:api.spellcheck.corp,run:rpc-clean-args;q=100;audit=temporary-dev-test|SIG:BASE64SIG
---

Validation flow (runtime)
1) parse envelope quickly (split on |).
2) check kid -> fetch cached public key for signer (cached map with TTL).
3) verify signature (one ed25519 verify). If fails, reject.
4) check exp/iat (allow skew up to 60s).
5) enforce scope: map capability atoms to runtime policies (e.g., map fs:r to VFS allow list).
6) decrement q (atomic fast path in memory) if present; if q exhausted, deny.
7) emit audit event with sub, scope, and token id (hash of payload).

Revocation strategy
- Prefer short TTLs (minutes) for kicked plugins. Longer-lived tokens for stable integrations but require revocation list checks.
- Revocation list: Bloom filter variant pushed to runtimes periodically (space efficient). Each CTL publishes periodic revocation bloom and a sequence number. Runtimes reject tokens whose payload-hash is in the bloom for the latest sequence; if bloom seq is stale, runtime may fallback to online check or deny depending on local policy.
- Emergency revoke: control-plane can mark a token id as emergency revoked; pushes immediate small update to streaming channel (pubsub) to active hosts.

Batching and quota semantics
- q field is a positive integer that the runtime decrements per usage unit (e.g., per tool call or per MB egress). Units are agreed on at mint time via the audit string or a linked policy id.
- To avoid racey cross-process decrements, token q is designed for approximate accounting: runtime keeps an in-memory counter checkpointed to local disk every N operations. Exactness is not required for many cases; for hard quotas, require server-hosted resources and a server-side check.

Tooling and control-plane mint API (sketch)
- POST /v1/plugin-tokens/mint
  - body: {"plugin_id":"acme","tenant":"acme-corp","scopes":["fs:r:/data/plugins/acme","net:e:api.spellcheck.corp"],"ttl_secs":3600,"quota":100,"audit":"ci/canary-run"}
  - response: {"token":"<compact-envelope>","token_id":"sha256(...)"}
- GET /v1/plugin-tokens/:token_id -> status, last_used, seq_revoked?
- POST /v1/plugin-tokens/revoke -> {token_id, reason}

Unresolved questions / TODOs (personal)
- Should we standardize on ed25519-only to keep crypto ops fast? Probably yes.
- Bloom false-positive rate tradeoffs for revocation; need simulation on typical token counts (10k-1M).
- Offline hosts: how to handle when bloom feed is lagging by days? Probably allow limp-mode where TTLs matter more and longer-lived tokens are forbidden in offline mode.
- Privacy: audit string might leak tenant/plugin intent; consider storing only policy id and keep human reason in control-plane logs.
- Path prefix semantics need canonicalization rules to avoid /data/ vs /data// vs symlink issues. Map to inode-range in host if possible.

Sketches for ascii diagram
- Minting flow:
  CONTROL-PLANE --> (mint token) --> PLUGIN REGISTRY
  CONTROL-PLANE --push rev bloom seq--> HOSTS (every 30s)
  PLUGIN (attaches token) -> RUNTIME -> validate -> allow tool / FS / NET

Notes to self: keep this simple for the first cut. Focus on ed25519 single-verify fast path + compact payload parsing. Later iterate on revocation scalability.

Local dev checklist
- [ ] prototype payload parser in Rust (nom) + verify using ring/ed25519-dalek
- [ ] simulate bloom update frequencies and FP rates for 100k tokens
- [ ] write small shim that maps scope -> VFS/egress policy and unit-tests path canonicalization
- [ ] write quick RFC for eng-sre and security review

End of sketch.
